title: A small, generic ‘preserve editorial intent’ prompt made outputs drift and failed promotion
description: A reusable editorial‑hierarchy instruction added to the Narrative user prompt did not preserve the supplied editorial intent; candidate runs consistently subordinated company identity and audience, made orchestration the central message, introduced unsupported claims, and the change was rejected and rolled back.
audience: Prompt engineers, Narrative/Compose maintainers, editorial leads responsible for model-driven outputs
rationale: This experiment is direct evidence that even short, generic prompt constraints can change the editorial hierarchy in systematic ways. For teams that control production prompts, the result argues for conservative change, controlled A/B testing, and hard promotion gates rather than assuming harmless reuse of editorial rules.
evidence:
• Candidate prompt added a single generic section “Preserve Editorial Intent from the Synthesis.” (Prompt diff in prompt-changes/Narrative.user.prompt.diff).
• Only Narrative.user.prompt.txt was changed; all other files, inputs, and model alias were identical.
• Candidate Narrative mean score 4.00/10 vs baseline 6.00/10; Compose mean 3.33/10 vs baseline 5.67/10 (tables in Run scores).
• All three candidate runs made orchestration central and introduced unsupported audience/validation framing (analysis section; failed gates C and D in every candidate run).
• Decision: “Do not promote.” Candidate not promoted; production prompt restored byte‑for‑byte (rollback SHA-256 match).

title: An explicit factual/editorial‑restraint gate prevented promotion — the value of hard gates
description: The experiment used a rubric with a hard promotion gate for factual/editorial restraint; candidate outputs repeatedly failed that gate (unsupported audience/commitments) and that single criterion alone blocked promotion.
audience: Release managers, QA leads, editorial policy owners, product managers overseeing model output governance
rationale: The scoring rubric treated factual/editorial restraint (no unsupported claims) as a hard gate. The candidate’s consistent failures on that criterion demonstrate how explicit, single-point checks can protect production from regressions even when other metrics (readability, coherence) look acceptable.
evidence:
• Scoring rubric: criterion D (Factual/editorial restraint) is a hard promotion gate (0–2 scoring described under Scoring rubric).
• Candidate Narrative and Compose runs repeatedly scored 0 or 1 on D; analysis: “No candidate run passed this gate. The Narrative outputs introduced validation intent/commitment, an audience of founders/product leaders/builders, or a need for coordinated AI.”
• Promotion decision cites failure on orchestration hierarchy and factual restraint as reasons: “Candidate was worse… failed the orchestration hierarchy and factual restraint gates in every run.”

title: Prompt‑only change, controlled experiment: evidence the Narrative prompt alone caused the regression
description: The experiment intentionally changed only the Narrative user prompt while keeping commit, inputs, other prompts, and model alias identical; the consistent decline across three candidate runs isolates the prompt change as the primary differing variable.
audience: Engineers and researchers running prompt‑sensitivity experiments, reproducibility-focused teams
rationale: When diagnosing regressions in model outputs, isolating variables is essential. This runset supplies a clear example of a minimal, controlled change (one prompt file) producing stable, repeatable regressions, supporting prompt‑first troubleshooting.
evidence:
• Repository and baseline verification: all files matched production by SHA‑256; only Narrative.user.prompt changed in candidate.
• Controlled comparison configuration: baseline reused prior outputs; candidate had three runs with only Narrative.user.prompt changed.
• Execution and inputs remained identical (same commit, model alias gpt-5-mini, same console workflow, same Compose format), per Controlled comparison section.
• Candidate runs’ scores were consistent (candidate Narrative SD 0.00), suggesting a stable effect from the prompt change.

title: Baseline Synthesis contained an internal tension between company identity and a later ‘orchestration is central’ line — a source of framing ambiguity
description: The baseline Synthesis paired Nuëyon’s company identity and Compose at top-level emphasis but also included a later line calling orchestration “central to the product direction,” creating an internal emphasis tension that the candidate prompt change amplified.
audience: Narrative prompt writers, editorial reviewers, product storytellers
rationale: Understanding preexisting ambiguities in a reference Synthesis helps explain why downstream outputs are sensitive to small prompt edits. Highlighting such internal tensions can guide prompt design and Synthesis editing to remove mixed signals before wider distribution.
evidence:
• Analysis: “The baseline Synthesis pairs company identity with Compose in its top-level emphasis, but also contains a later description calling orchestration ‘central to the product direction.’”
• The document notes this internal tension may have “reinforced the technical angle,” though it explicitly states this observation does not change the controlled result.
• Baseline runs still showed variability on theme hierarchy (baseline C scores 1,0,0), indicating the baseline Synthesis was not wholly unambiguous.

title: Operational practice: fast rollback with byte‑for‑byte verification preserved production integrity
description: After the candidate failed evaluation, the team restored the production Narrative user prompt byte‑for‑byte, verified builds and tests passed, and recorded hashes and artifacts — demonstrating a concise rollback and verification workflow.
audience: DevOps engineers, release managers, platform reliability teams
rationale: A documented rollback and verification process reduces risk when experiments fail. The artifact list, SHA‑256 verification, and successful builds/tests provide a concrete example of conservative operational practice around prompt changes.
evidence:
• Decision: “Do not promote.” Production prompt restored from saved byte snapshot; rollback verification: production prompt SHA‑256 equals the frozen baseline hash.
• Builds: dotnet build passed with 0 warnings/errors; tests: 165 passed, 0 failed/0 skipped.
• Artifact index lists baseline/candidate outputs, prompt diffs, and metadata.json capturing hashes and execution IDs.
